utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. May we begin by taking the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Tom Hannis, Gerard Dobbyn, and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Cvijetic, Mr. O'Sullivan, and Zecevic for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I promised that I would finish within 15 minutes, but it might take a bit longer. But I think it will assist the Trial Chamber, the line of the cross-examination, so with your leave I will proceed with the witness a bit longer than anticipated. I'm sorry for that, but I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess half an hour all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. I would remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Panic. Are you well?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, yesterday we talked about the prisons in Zvornik. I showed you a number of orders and instructions from the Ministry of the Interior relating to this issue. Let me remind you, I showed you a letter dated the 10th of August, then the one dated the 17th of August which we commented yesterday, and now I would like to show you a letter -- or rather, an instruction dated 24th of August in which the Ministry of the Interior is again making a query and asking for information. That's Exhibit 1D57, if we can please have that on our screens. The Ministry of the Interior, based on the letter from the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare of the government from whom they had received requests for information is now passing on to all public security stations and Public Security Service centres this document requiring the following information: The name and the location of a camp, who ordered the camp to be established, who ordered the individuals to be detained there, the number of detainees, the number of the people arrested, and they gave them the dead-line for providing this information by the 30th of August, 1992. Have you ever seen this document, or do you know that the public security station in Zvornik has ever received this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this particular document. All I know is that people who were working in the medical institutions used to come to Novi Izvor prison. There was a female doctor. I think her name was Bela, but I don't know her full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the information about the existence of the prisons in Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour courts had been submitted as per requests from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, and I know that since this request arrived an answer should have been sent, and they had to be told about the doctors working in various institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the food provided at these two prisons, Novi Izvor and misdemeanours court. If I understood you correctly it seems that there was a centralised kitchen providing food in Zvornik for these facilities?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all received food, I say we and the hotel prisons from the hotel kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence -- yes, I apologise. Yes, it already has an exhibit number. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday I didn't object to a couple of documents, but this one I do have an objection. The witness hasn't seen this document. He doesn't really have anything to add to it. I would oppose this one at this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies for creating any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, Mr. Panic, while we were talking you said that either from the beginning or from mid-August, all these collection centres, camps, prisons, whatever, ceased to exist except for the basic prison in Novi Izvor, or rather, misdemeanours court, and all the detainees had been handed over to the army and taken to the Batkovic camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only this prison remained I think until the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, the Prosecutor showed you a document 65 ter 1585. I suppose it's been given a P number now, but unfortunately I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document pulled up, this document. 65 ter 1585.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] So that's P342.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember seeing this document when the Prosecutor showed it to you in which a certain Colonel Ilic, despite all this warning coming from the MUP and other state organs and the decisions taken in this respect, orders the Muslims from the Divic collection centre, 78 men to be handed over on the 22nd -- 29 August 1992. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this document, and I said that I didn't know this Colonel Ilic. He probably was from the corps because their command was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you know at all that there was any kind of collection centre in Divic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was Divic or the residents of Divic who were first in the centre in Celopek, and some of them were injured by maltreatment, were sent back to Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour courts. I don't know any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here "Divic collection centre, 78 people," shows that by the end of August it was under the army's control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember stating earlier to the Prosecutor, I said that there was a collection centre at the football playground in Divic, only I don't know whether in this period or not. And Slavko Eric used to take Muslims to Olovske Luke. Some of them remained there, and the rest were brought back in two or three buses, and Miko Miljanovic put those people in Celopek, but I can't give you any time-frame for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that after these problems the rampaging by Repic and the others in the Celopek centre, the people who were transferred to Novi Izvor and the misdemeanours court, as you said, injured and wounded, they were transferred there in order to be protected and in order to receive medical treatment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P347. That's a report on the work of the Zvornik SJB. That's a quarterly report covering July, August, and September 1992. On the last page you can see that it was signed by the then-chief Milorad Lokancevic. And on page 1, the last two sentences of the third paragraph, it reads as follows, just to say that this document was drafted I suppose in late September or early October. And it reads as follows: "Also, a number of measures were undertaken relating to collection centres that -- and there are two such centres in the municipality housing 180 persons. This problem has been passed on to all the military organs, CSB, MUP, and the Ministry of Health, but everything remained as it is. It was only on the 18th of September of this year that with the assistance of military organ the collection centre in Divic was disbanded, where 90 people were, mainly women, elderly, and children, while in the prison in Zvornik there are still 56 people." As far as I understand, on the 18th of September, this colonel in his previous letter now says that it has been disbanded. In other words, that means that the SJB Zvornik played a role in this Divic centre for more than two weeks, approximately.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the letter and the information, I have no reason to doubt that. I don't know whether they wanted to go to Olovske Luke and those who didn't were put into the Novi Izvor prison, but as far as this information goes I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in conclusion, on the 18th of September onwards, in the territory of Zvornik municipality and under the jurisdiction of the SJB, there was only this so-called basic prison in Zvornik in Novi Izvor and the misdemeanours court. And that was it. Based on this letter, we can conclude that nothing else existed in that sense. Later on a commission from the Ministry of Judiciary and Administration came and confirmed that. Can you confirm that for me?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is of course an important piece of information that by 18th of September there was only the Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court remaining as detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the witness also said that all the other detention centres that existed in the Zvornik area prior to 18th September were closed down one by one and that the detainees there were transferred to Batkovic. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. That's the evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it leaves me with the impression that Batkovic then must have been an enormous camp. How many people were there, or were people released or in -- what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Batkovic camp was a military facility; therefore, we have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, you heard the question. Do you know anything at all about the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it. As far as Batkovic is concerned, I only know that the prisoners were transferred to the Batkovic camp, and this is where exchanges took place of certain detainees with Tuzla. As for anything else, I don't know what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, are you able to give us an impression of the number of detainees that were transferred to Batkovic and the number of detainees who were then held at Novi Izvor and at the misdemeanour court after 18 September? I'm interested in getting an impression of the number of persons that we are talking about here. Maybe I should ask first of all: Do you know how many detention centres were closed down prior to 18th September 1992? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said as for Batkovic I really cannot tell you very much because it was done by the military service, and I know the technical centre, Ekonomija, the brickworks factory, Novi Izvor, and the misdemeanours court. I also cannot tell you how many people were detained there, but what was left behind were some 30, 40 individuals. I think that concerning Novi Izvor could -- Sredo Vukovic who was running the Novi Izvor could give you more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So can I just ask you if I have understood correctly the following information, namely, that in the period leading up to 18 September 1992, three or maybe four detention centres were closed down and the prisoners -- or the detainees at those detention centres were transferred to Batkovic, and by 18 September only 30 or 40 detainees remained at Novi Izvor and at the misdemeanour court. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. After the war I saw a number of those prisoners from Batkovic or who were in Celopek prison. I saw them and I talked to them. Those were the people who were exchanged, and there were many of them who were exchanged at Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Just one final question. I think that during your testimony we heard of a significantly higher number of detainees at Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court, I think several hundred but I'm not sure. Can you tell us, if you know, what happened to those detainees from Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court. Were they also sent to Batkovic so that by 18 September we only had 30 or 40 detainees left there? I don't know if I made myself clear, but if there were many more people detained before 18th September at Novi Izvor, what happened to those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a lot of these prisoners were transferred to Batkovic as well. I think that one of them was even exchanged for a Serb from Sarajevo, and this man from Divic was known as the Frenchman because his father used to work in France. What I said was that sometime in January 1993 that there were 20 or 30 prisoners were allegedly taken to cut wood but were executed there. But I really cannot tell you the exact figure, maybe 30, 40, maybe even 50 because I never went to that prison and I never looked at any lists. This is what I heard second-hand from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And one final question. I apologise, Mr. Zecevic. Am I also right to understand from what you have told us that it was the minister of the MUP who took the decisions to have all of these detainees assembled at Batkovic and have the remaining centres closed down? I mean, this was -- this entire operation was done under the control of the minister of MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was under the control of the MUP minister. If the dispatches and letters came from the ministry, they were received by the chief and the chief was the one who implemented all those instructions and orders. I didn't see any of them. By the rule, such things should be sent from the ministry downwards and distributed from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] If I may be of any assistance to you, Your Honours, the document that I showed you just a moment ago P347 alleges that in the prison - and I'm talking about a report for July, August, and September - where it is alleged that in the Zvornik prison there were 56 persons and that would be the exact and correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I'm a bit confused now. All the three documents from the MUP that I showed you yesterday and the one that I just showed you today, they are not directives of any kind. Those are directives to submit information about the existence of the place or anything to the contrary, and that was your testimony, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Whoever was in charge should have submitted all that information and data.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we understand each other in that. Batkovic, Batkovic, and the entire operation to transfer prisoners from Zvornik to Batkovic was a hundred per cent military operation? Am I right in thinking that? I believe that this is your testimony, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the transfer of prisoners from Zvornik to Batkovic was something that had nothing whatsoever to do with the police. The police did not have a role to play in that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Panic, we have another topic that I would like to discuss with you, and I believe that it will be of some significance and assistance to the Trial Chamber. The document number is 65 ter 1793. It was admitted yesterday, but again because of an error on my computer I was not able to record the P number. Could I ask you to help me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P348.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Chamber please produce that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the work for the year 1992. I believe that you were present when I objected to the admission of this document into evidence, and I therefore wanted to discuss some things with you. Mr. Panic, in the police you spent your entire career, as it were. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many official annual report does a public security station submit to the responsible security services centre every year, either to the security services centre or to the ministry, how many one or more?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is just one annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about annual reports, exclusively about annual reports. I know that there are other reports such as daily, quarterly, and so on and so forth, but I would like to focus on annual reports. My question to you is this: How many annual reports are submitted every year? That's my question, is there one or more?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at the document together, the document is on the screen. On page 1, this is obviously an attachment to the document where it says "1992," under 1, methodology for drafting the report, under 2 report, under 3 programme of activities for the year 1993. Am I right, have I read all that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page number 2 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you're going to see that page, and could you please confirm that the page depicts the programme of work for the year 1993. Can you see that? Is that a customary form that was used to draft the annual programme of work? Would that be its first page?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything depended on the drafter. Maybe this was normal for this particular person who authored this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 12 in e-court is where this document ends. Page 12 of this document is the end of the programme of work. You will see that it shows the name of the chief of the service but the document is not signed. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 13 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at this. This is a document that was submitted to the CSB Bijeljina. The document number in the left upper corner is 01-16-01-06-2. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The date is 8 January 1993, and this is a supplement of the work report of the Zvornik SJB for the year 1992. And it says that it is connected with a document under the same number as this one dated 7 January 1993, and further on it says that the supplement is being sent in order to clarify some of the tasks and duties within the purview of traffic police. And the signature is by the chief of the SJB, Milorad Lokancevic. Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says so. The programme did not include the work of the traffic security police, and that's why a supplement is being submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the following page, page number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an accompanying letter, again, bearing the same number as the previous document 01-16/01-061-2. And the date is 4th of January, 1993. And the document was sent to the CSB Bijeljina -- do you want us to take a break?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is all down to cigarettes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, take your time. Take it easy. Could you follow what I've just told you?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the document is a report on the work of the SJB Zvornik for 1992 and the work programme for 1993, and it was sent to the CSB in Bijeljina and the CSB in Sarajevo. Can you see that? And it was signed by Chief Milorad Lokancevic. Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's show the witness page number 15 in the same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document bears the same number as the previous two documents. I'm not going to repeat it. And the date is 7 January 1993. The document was sent to the CSB in Sarajevo, and again it refers to the report on the work of the SJB Zvornik for the year 1992. Again, this document is signed by Milorad Lokancevic, and you can see on the left-hand side that the document was sent to the Bijeljina CSB, Sarajevo CSB, and archives. And in handwriting you can see that it was sent by Telex via Pale on the 9th of January, 1993. Can you see all that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now show the witness page 16 in the same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 16 in the same document is a report on the work of the Zvornik SJB for the year 1992, and the number -- or rather, the date it bears is January 1993. If you scroll down just a little we'll all be able to see the date. Could you please scroll down. January 1993 is the date. And it says that it was sent by Telex via Pale on the 9th of January, 1993. And finally you will see the signature of the chief, Chief Lokancevic. Do you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document that we see now - and the pages are between 16 and 28 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would kindly ask the witness to be shown page 21 of the document. Page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see this is page 21, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we blow up the whole page a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It speaks about the participation of MUP members in combat operations, the tasks and duties of the police, and so on and so forth. Could you please take a look at this page, sir, and then we will move on to the next one. I would like you to compare the page that you have before you now and the one that I'm just about to show you. Have you had enough time to look at the page, sir? I'm interested in hearing from you whether this document was typed on two different typewriters. Could you please take a careful look at this page, and then you will look at page 26. Did you have a good look?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 22 in e-court. Again, blow up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to agree with me, Mr. Panic, that this was typed on a totally different typewriter and that on page 6 the number looks very much like figure 8?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're not able to say that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The numbers are different. It says "SJB" and -- no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown pages 21 and 22 at the same time on the screen, both in the Serbian language. So could two different pages be displayed on the screen at the same time, 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at these two pages and please tell me whether you would be agreeable to say that the typewriters are different and the font is different. Maybe the two pages could be blown up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, whereas I understand the thrust of the questions that you're putting to the witness, having regard to his -- he doesn't -- he doesn't purport to hold any expertise in typewriter style and print, wouldn't the submissions be just as effective once you at the appropriate stage make it to the Chamber, who would have the -- in other words, it seems to me that the witness has no greater ability than the Chamber would have in this regard to the extent that this is an important point for your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with Your Honours, and I understand the position. I was just trying because I believe the witness is an experienced policeman, that he should be able to assist us on this. If Your Honour feels that this can be achieved by a submission, I'm perfectly willing to stop the cross-examination on this subject with the witness and make the submission in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it will assist the Chamber and my learned friend, I'll stipulate that those two pages appear to be typed on different typewriters. He's an experienced police officer, but we have no evidence that he's an experienced report preparer or a typist or anything of that nature. And I really don't think he can assist us much. If that's the point Mr. Zecevic wants to make, I agree, we can all look at that and see it was done on two different machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the concern is the fact I went at depth yesterday to analyse this document because I made the objection and it was overruled and the document was admitted. And I'm trying to, if I can, to assist the Trial Chamber because now it comes to the weight of the document. What I'm trying to is to show the Trial Chamber that there is a -- there is a substantial question on the authenticity of these documents because they are completely different reports. And I wanted just to establish through the witness. If I can, I'm perfectly willing to do that by submission in due course when the Court pleases. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We remember your objection from yesterday, and we do understand that you want to point out the differences between the two parts of this document. Now, you have taken the witness to a number of pages in the reports, but I'm unsure about the purpose for doing this. You took the witness from one page to the next to the next and so on, but what are the points that you would wish to highlight in showing these pages or passages to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly what I said just now, that this document contains two annual reports for 1992 of SJB Zvornik which are completely and in a very substantial part different. There is a difference in statistical data, there is a difference in comments, in everything. They are entirely two different documents which are contained in one exhibit right now. And that was the point of my objection yesterday. Now, when I analysed it, I indeed analysed it in depth, I am perfect -- I have now all the major discrepancies now, and I wanted to go with the witness through this. If, as I say, the Trial Chamber feels that this can be done by submission, I'm perfectly willing to terminate my cross-examination and make the submission in due course whenever it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe I have just been unattentive or not paid particular -- sufficient attention to the pages that you showed to the witness, but it is at this moment a bit unclear to me which differences exactly you wish to point out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, namely, the document which is -- this part of the document, so to speak, is contained in the pages 16 to 28 in the e-court. That is the -- that is the report of -- for SJB -- the annual report for SJB Zvornik dated January 1993. This document -- this document contains 12 pages. The next document which is also called the report for SJB Zvornik dated December has 13 pages. These two documents are completely different reports for the same period of time and for the same SJB Zvornik, and that is what I intended to show through the witness. It contains completely different data. It contains completely different matters. So that's why I say it is -- this document will not assist the Trial Chamber because we cannot be sure which one of these reports is the real annual report. I -- my submission is that these reports are not sufficiently -- this document is not sufficiently authenticated that we can't use it properly, because we don't know which one of these was the official. It might be that both are maybe versions of the document which didn't -- which didn't after all became an official report. That is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Now, as I recall from my reading the documents, the two versions are not entirely different. Parts have been added in one and some new information has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my submission is that the documents are entirely different, and I can prove that to you. But I don't think that it needs -- it would need a significant amount of court time. Maybe I can do that in a submission -- in a written submission, and indicate exactly the points where there is discrepancies between the two documents, which I think are important and relevant of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Like number of killings, like the existence of the war crimes. In one there is no mentioning of war crimes; in the other there are three criminal complaints filed for the war crimes. I mean, that's, in my opinion, is very relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. I get the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be thrilled to discuss some of those issues, but we don't need to do it with this witness. He can't contribute to this. He wasn't a report writer. He doesn't know anything about that. If there was something specific Mr. Zecevic had to say about -- report one lists 23 patrolmen and report two lists 28 he might be able to ask this witness and say, how many were there, and if he could say 23 or 28, but absent something like that, it's a waste of all our time to be trying to do this with him. This should be a submission -- and I would argue, you already decided that this was admissible. His arguments now should go to weight, and that's something we can save for the end of the case or another day, but we shouldn't be doing it now in the courtroom with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree, Mr. Hannis, with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions from Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then may I proceed with re-direct, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll deal with a few questions from today first, Mr. Panic, and then go to some things from yesterday. At page 4, line 8 today Mr. Zecevic asked you about all the camps ceasing to exist. And you told us earlier about there were hundreds of people detained in these various collection centres and camps from the beginning of the war, and you've given us some evidence to indicate several hundreds were killed and buried in mass graves. And I think you told us about Mr. Tanic, a police employee, who was involved in identifying some of the bodies and bagging the bodies. That's right, Mr. Tanic was a police employee and did that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was employed with the police, and he was appointed to the commission for sanitation and hygiene clearance of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to get down to the 30 or 40 or 50 that were left in September, I guess hundreds of others were exchanged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then the rest were sent to Batkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But weren't many of the Muslims that were being held in detention in Zvornik civilians and not prisoners of war, not fighters?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in most cases that referred to the technical school centre, primarily the case was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at least we know from Colonel Ilic's order that we looked at yesterday, that those at the Divic centre were civilians because that was the purpose of his order saying these aren't military people; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the residents of Divic were for the most part civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And at page 11 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 11 Mr. Zecevic asked you about Batkovic and he said: "So we understand each other in that, Batkovic and the entire operation to transfer prisoners from Zvornik to Batkovic was a hundred per cent military operation. Am I right in thinking that?" And your answer was: "Yes, that's what I stated." And he goes on to say: "That means the transfer to Batkovic was something that had nothing whatsoever to do with the police. The police did not have a role to play in that." You said: "You're right." But didn't the police at least have a role in opening the doors to Novi Izvor so the military could come in and pick up those people? The police had to do something for that transfer to occur; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as Novi Izvor or any other prison where police was providing security, they would receive orders how many people should be handed over to the army, and how it would help with the military trucks and the soldiers who came there. That is the level of the police participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And would the police hand over civilians to the military to take them to a military camp without any documentation to indicate that they were prisoners of war, that is, combatants?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Always a document should be received beforehand, and probably the chief or the commander receives such a document, who then informed the prison warden who is going to be handed over to the army to be taken to Batkovici. So that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to go back to yesterday. At page 2978, line 7, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about Dragan Spasojevic, and you told us that he worked at the police just a bit over a year. And how old was he? I understand he was a pretty young man in 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was born in either 1964 or 1966, I'm not sure, but yes he was younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why such a young man with so little experience in the police was given the job of commander rather than some older, more experienced guy like yourself? What was his qualification for the job?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an SDS member from the very beginning, and he was in the Main Board. I was not an SDS member, and these things were decided along the party lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next at page 3006, beginning at line 18, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the special brigade who came to make the arrest of the paramilitaries. Do you know how many men came in that special brigade unit for that purpose approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact number because they came during the night. We were ordered not to leave the hotel. They arrested them, took them to Bijeljina, and we never saw them again until some of the groups returned again sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Zecevic was asking you whether or not the -- given the nature of these groups and the nature of the problem, whether it was appropriate that some time would be required to plan and organise such an operation. And you agreed with him. It was not something that would be appropriate for an ad hoc operation. But my question is: In Zvornik you had had problems with Zuco and the other paramilitaries a long time before the 20th of July; right? They'd been a problem from the very beginning in April?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we saw in a report by a couple of inspectors, Mr. Andan and the other gentleman dated 17 June, that the inspectors were aware of the problem in the middle of June. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you -- I think you'd told us you had heard about the incident where Minister Ostojic was stopped at the check-point and taken out of his car. Do you recall that that was sometime in July?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in July, but I'm not sure about the specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Next at page 3012, line 16, Mr. Zecevic asked you regarding Repic and those crimes he was committing against the detained in Celopek, he said: "Do you know that due to the nature of the crimes involved, these are crimes that are violations of international humanitarian law. In the law of war in the former Yugoslavia it was military organs that dealt with this?" And you said: "Yes. As far as military personnel were concerned, they were tried by military courts."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC SAID
utterances.text: "Not only with regard to military personnel, also with regard to these particular forms of crime that were committed in a situation of war?" And you said: "Yes." But did you know about the law about war crimes in the newly formed Republika Srpska? Was there any change between the old law and the new law, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with any new laws, whether there were any changes or not. I know only that Repic was later tried and convicted in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even under the old Yugoslav criminal law, wasn't it possible for certain crimes, like the murder of the Muslim civilians in Celopek Dom, could not a crime like that be charged either as a regular murder under the criminal code or as a war crime? Didn't the Prosecutor have discretion, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably had, but why I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know -- my -- I'm not sure about this, but do you know whether or not there was a longer penalty, prison sentence, for a regular murder than for a war crime, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I think that the penalty for a war crime should be longer, but that's my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And even if it was something that might be defined as a war crime, if you as a policeman had knowledge of it would you have an obligation to report it to somebody, no matter whether it was committed by a military person or a civilian or a policeman? If you knew about it, would you have an obligation to report?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I would have reported it, but as for the army and their jurisdiction and everything to do with them, it was up to the military police. At that time, when all these paramilitary formations were so strong, I have very strong doubts that they would dare report them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally ever report any crimes you were aware of to the military authorities or the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen any crime or any murder, only what I said in my statement was that I saw Repic coming in and therefore I wouldn't make a good witness. However, the witness -- the army authority and its officers knew very well what the military was doing, particularly in the area of Zvornik. The situation was normalised. We were back to our regular duties of maintaining law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 3013, line 20, Mr. Zecevic asked you about the special unit coming back to Zvornik after the Yellow Wasps and the others had already been arrested and detained. You don't have any personal knowledge yourself about why the special unit came back after that operation was completed, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Occasionally a few number from Bijeljina would come passing by or if they decided to come to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Talking about Repic at page 3016, line 5, you were asked about your view about the reserve policemen vis-à-vis Mr. Repic, and the question was: "And knowing the structure of his personality, I mean he did not mind who was of which ethnicity, there was his readiness to mistreat and kill anyone for any reason; right?" And your answer was: "Precisely." My question is: First of all, at Celopek how many guards were there? How many reserve policemen were guarding that facility, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two or three, whereas the rest were at the school or on patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the information you got from your colleague there about Repic coming, what was your understanding? Did Repic come alone or with one or two friends or in a large group?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They always appeared in troikas or in twos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the guards, the reserve police, were armed with automatic rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Repic do anything to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never met with him. I didn't see him, maybe just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you never heard of him doing anything to a Serb, only the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. However, judging by the rumours about him it is possible. I suppose that they did not dare oppose him, and even if a Serb had opposed them I suppose that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't know of any instance where a Serb or a Serb policeman ever opposed him or he ever mistreated a Serb or a Serb policeman; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how long the delay was in moving the Celopek survivors after the police first became aware that Repic had abused them and mutilated the genitals of some of them and committed those other atrocities? How long did it take before they got moved to someplace a little safer? Was it weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I believe that it was less than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 3017, line 9, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the nature of prisons in Bosnia and the former Yugoslavia, how they're established and who guards them. In Zvornik, from the beginning of the conflict when the paramilitaries and the TO and these other groups were capturing people and setting up these -- I guess the best definition is that one that was in Mr. Stanisic's comments in the July meeting in Belgrade, these undefined camps, they weren't really arresting them in the strict legal sense that you as a policeman arrest somebody, were they?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. No procedure was followed, no normal police procedure. They arrested them and they established the camps. They incarcerated them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these places where these people put were not really prisons in the strict legal technical legal sense like Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court might have been a prison. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the facilities where they were incarcerated was a real prison. Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court served as prisons before the war, so they could be referred to as prisons in a certain manner. And the others were mostly factories, schools, and other such makeshift facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Gogic and Crni, were they also capturing some people or arresting people and bringing them into detention, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, but I heard that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us they were wearing police uniforms and being paid out of the police budget; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they never brought them to Novi Izvor, for example, or to the police station where there was a room where people were interviewed. I don't know where they took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In the MUP quarterly report for April, May, and June, that's Exhibit P322, Your Honours, there was an -- there was one entry that said that during this time-period police employees brought in 537 and interviewed 48 Muslim extremists. Does that number include people brought in by Gogic and Crni, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that that number includes those; however, those who were brought for interviews were brought in by the police and the military to a certain extent. And then crime prevention police inspectors or inspectors from the state security would interview these people and decide as to what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In terms of these other detention facilities or undefined camps, I believe you told us in your testimony before that some people were detained for a while at least at the Celopek Dom, Drinjaca school, Standard, Alhos, and Karakaj Technical School. Were there any others that I've missed or that you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ekonomija, yes, the brickworks; Novi Izvor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Ciglane I forgot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's nearly time for the break. I have probably 10 or 15 more minutes. So I don't know if you want me to continue for a while or recess now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If this is a convenient point -- because as you say you're just maybe two minutes early of the break, but if this is a convenient point --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and you can't complete before the break, we may as well break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Our delay in taking the bench following the break was dealing with certain administrative matters which relate to the hearing, as counsel would appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I just have a few more questions for you. At page 3019, line 23, Mr. Zecevic was showing you a document and he said: "Here it says that the army was taking into detention or bringing into detention members of the public and population without any documents and then left such camps to the Ministry of the Interior." And you were asked if that was the situation in Zvornik. And he went on to ask you: "So you also knew that there were no documents supporting the detention of such individuals were found by the police once they took over; that's right?" And you said: "No, only later did the prison, wardens, and guards start keeping records of events." My question is: When the police took over some of these non-standard detention facilities or these undefined camps and you had no records for the people that were there, shouldn't they have been released if there were no documents to support their detention, just as a procedural matter? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question. However, whether they should have been released or not, they could not have taken that decision without the superior officer, and I suppose the officer appointed a warden, guards, ordered them to keep the records of daily events, and everything else that was a standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I understand your answer to mean that you don't believe that the guards at that level had the authority to release the people; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But generally speaking based on your experience as a policeman, people can't be kept in detention without some kind of criminal charges or some finding by a judge, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the book, that should have been the case. They should have been interviewed, they should have been said why they were brought in, they should have been informed as to what was being alleged against them, they should have been handed over to a court or a prosecutor's office, but that was simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, at page 3026, beginning at line 22, Mr. Zecevic had asked you if you knew about any incidents where paramilitaries had broken in to some of these detention facilities guarded by the police and abused the prisoners. And you said: "I know about that. I did not see it, but I heard, for example, that a military policeman came in, the previous day his brother had been killed and he entered with a rifle, disarmed the guard, and beat some Muslims." Which facility was that at, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was in Novi Izvor. I'm not sure that our active or reserve policeman was on duty or whether it was a military police policeman whose brother had been killed. In any case, as far as I remember his name was Slavko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was, what month?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say. It was 17 years ago. It was in 1992, very early in 1992, but I can't be sure of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far was that Novi Izvor facility from the SJB building in Zvornik, how many metres or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty metres, immediately behind the police building. Between the police building and Novi Izvor there were some depots, the misdemeanour court, and then behind the two there was the Novi Izvor -- administrative building of Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding that incident, do you know whether the guard or the warden or yourself, did anybody inform the military police about that incident?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I probably heard that only a month or so after the event. Either the guard or the warden should have reported that. If they were members of our police, they should have reported that incident to the public security station, and alternatively if they were military police then they should have reported that to the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, on Wednesday, I think, and it's transcript page 54 -- just one moment. 53, 25 -- 53, 25, yes, you were asked: "With regard to equipment that regular policemen in Zvornik had, what kind of uniforms and weapons did you have in April, May, June, July 1992?" Your answer is: "We had multi-coloured camouflage uniforms in olive-drab." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had both camouflage and olive-drab uniforms and we also had blue camouflage uniforms. When we were engaged, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. You -- indeed I should have finished your -- the answer. You indeed said "and police uniforms." But then my question is as follows: If someone would say that he have seen people or units wearing olive-drab uniforms and therefore he makes the conclusion that that must have been military and not police people or units, he could have been wrong because you were wearing olive-drab uniforms as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible those who were not familiar with uniforms didn't know that military uniforms were different. They were more intense green, whereas ours had more white in the pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. I would like to just return briefly to the matter of closing down these undefined camps and transferring the detainees from there to the Batkovic military prison. And my question is: Why was it decided to close down the camps and transfer the detainees to Batkovic, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a correct and honest answer. It was up to my superiors, and at the time I may not even have been there. I was sent all over the place. To be honest, I really can't -- I may make a mistake. I don't know who took that decision. I know that it was somebody above me, a higher instance. I only heard that they were transferred. Who ordered that, who arranged that, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic, for your attendance to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish you a pleasant stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Di Fazio has the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please, the next witness is Mr. Majkic, Dragan Majkic, and I call him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I ask you your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Majkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your -- and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6 September 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever testify before this Court before or before any court in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, three times in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well then, as you are a witness called by the Prosecutor's office, they will start putting questions to you; afterwards, the Defence will; and eventually, the Judges may have some questions for you. I forgot one detail. Your profession, please? What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a mechanical engineer with a university degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, just to continue on with those personal details, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm a fire inspector, cantonal fire inspector in the canton of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And fire inspectors, are they -- do they work with the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: A few years ago we became civil servants, therefore we are not police employees any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. I just wanted to put some more personal details to you, and could you tell us if they're correct. You've given us your date of birth and your ethnicity. You were born in the village of Podug, which is about 3 or 4 kilometres from Sanski Most. You're a widower, and you have two children; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. You were educated in Sanski Most, and you did an engineering course at a place called Rijeka University, and in 1994 you started working at a place called the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry if I said "1994." I meant 1984. Thank you for that. In 1987 you joined the police as an inspector of fire protection, and in July of 1991 you were appointed as chief of police in Sanski Most. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you held that position as chief of police until very late April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the 18th of November -- sorry, my apologies. You joined the SDS political party prior to the November 1990 elections in Bosnia, and you left the party in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some personalities in the -- that you may know. Do you know Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you remember when you first met him, when you first were introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: That was probably seven or eight days after I had been appointed chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named -- or did you know a gentleman named Nedeljko Rasula or Rasula?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he hold any position in the SDS in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: He was the first president of the SDS Municipal Board in Sanski Most, and he was an MP in the BH parliament and also the president of the Assembly of Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Municipal Board of the SDS in Sanski Most, was that occasionally known as the principal -- the principal board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: No. The principal or the Main Board was at the very top of the SDS. I'm talking here about municipal boards that had their own Executive Boards at the level of local government, that is to say at the level of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1990, can you recall if there was an Executive Board at a municipal level in Sanski Most; and if so, who were the members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: First an initiating board was established, and it worked on the preparations for establishing the Municipal Board of the SDS in Sanski Most where the Municipal Board was elected, and Mr. Rasula was elected president of this board for Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Dusan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a doctor. He was a physician working at the clinic in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he on the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the Executive Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to run some names past you, and I want you to tell the Trial Chamber if you know these people and if they were members of the Executive Board in Sanski Most. Boro Savanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Nemanja Tripkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Drago Djuric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mico Prastalo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I think that he was, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Slobodan Krunic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And yourself, what about yourself, were you a member of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Vlado Vrkes, or did you know a gentleman named Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he occupy any position in the SDS in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: In 1990, when the Municipal Board had already been formed, at a meeting held in the village of Tomina - I think that was prior to the elections - Rasula brought him to this meeting and nominated him to be elected the secretary of the SDS in Sanski Most. We were slightly against this. We protested because nobody knew him; however, he said that, "If this man is not elected secretary, I will not continue to be your president." Therefore, we had no choice but to accept this nomination made by Mr. Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just earlier in your testimony this morning you mentioned that the Main Board or principal board, I'll refer to it as the Main Board of the SDS for Bosnia, was that located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How was policy formulated in the SDS, or perhaps my question should be more refined and I should ask you: Who formulated policy in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, you had Mr. Karadzic up there. He was one of the founding members of the SDS at the level of the republic. Then at his initiative, or I don't know exactly how, municipal or regional boards of the SDS were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Incidentally, was there a regional board in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It existed there before we even started with our initiative board in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Just cast your mind back to the period of time before the elections in 1990. How did the Sanski Most local SDS explain policy to the people in that period of time leading up to the elections?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me start from the beginning. A group of some 20 men, including myself, got together. Three of them somehow chaired this meeting. They said that they had been with Mr. Karadzic some month or month and a half with him, and that they discussed the idea of establishing the SDS in Sanski Most. Mr. Karadzic approved the idea, and they called one or two persons each from every village and they got together in the social club of the local commune in Sanski Most. And that was when it was agreed to establish the SDS in Sanski Most. In the village of Tramosnja the initiative on the steering committee was elected, Mr. Rasula was elected chairman, and after that a decision was made to establish boards in local communes. Then the presidents of subcommittees in local communes were later appointed to the executive committee of the municipality, and then later at the founding meeting of the SDS which was held in the sports hall, all these subcommittee presidents became members of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me perhaps explain myself a little better. In the period of time when you were electioneering, carrying out election activities, how did you explain to the local people, to the villagers, what SDS policy was? How did you tell them what the SDS stood for? What did you rely on? Did you have any documentation to assist you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: There was no documentation available. Everybody knew that single-party system of the communist rule was abolished, and a decision was made to introduce a multi-party system. And this idea was embraced by everyone. It was possible to establish all kinds of political parties, just like the League of Communists transformed itself into the SDB, or the Socialist Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Main Board of the SDS in Sarajevo ever provide the Sanski Most SDS with written documentation concerning official policy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Of course we had a platform or a manifesto and the statute of the SDS. This is what every political party had. It was probably Mr. Rasula who was at the head of this steering committee, had the statute, that he operated pursuant to this statute as well as to the programme and manifesto at the level of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Rasula ever go to Sarajevo to attend meetings with the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I know that he went there, and he informed us always about these trips, and then he would provide some feedback information, whether any instructions were given by the Main Board to be implemented or adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Rasula acted as a go-between, so to speak, between the SDS in Sanski Most and the Main Board in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Initially, there was a regional board of the SDS, and above it was the Main Board. Rasula used to go to meetings, both at the regional board and also at the Main Board when invited. I don't know how he appeared there, in what capacity, as a member of the Main Board, but he always went and he always told us what tasks or what instructions had been issued at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. During these meetings, either in Banja Luka at the regional board or the Main Board in Sarajevo, do you know if he had contact and discussions with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, he -- yes, he was later elected at this first multi-party elections an MP for the BH parliament. But I really don't know whether he met with him head to head. Once he asked me to come with him because I was already nominated for this appointment to the chief, he never met with Rasula. There was some discourse between regions and Mr. Karadzic, but at the end of the day everything ended normally at the meeting, ended normally. And then I did not notice Mr. Rasula meeting with anybody. He was at the meeting just like I was. Everybody was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Apart from meetings that you attended personally, did Mr. Rasula report to you that he had had discussions with Mr. Karadzic on occasions when he attended the regional board or the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: He never said that to me personally. He would talk about it at the meetings of the municipal board or of the Executive Board, which was formed later. He just reported to us whenever he -- any contacts were at the regional or the republican level. As I said, he never reported to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when the Executive Board in Sanski Most was reduced in size, the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. When the statute was amended, as far as I can remember, it was necessary to establish within the Executive Board a smaller operative body so that there would be no need to convene the meetings of the Executive Board always, and that was called Registry. And that smaller body -- because they had 11 members, and if necessary then the entire membership of the executive body would attend meetings. But that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember when that happened, what year that was or month if you can?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: It might have been in June 1991 or maybe July. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us if in this reduced and more compact Registry created from within the Executive Board, whether Rasula and Vrkes were members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were a member?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it had approximately 11 members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Not approximately, exactly 11 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And another member of that smaller, reduced body was also Boro Savanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, I don't think there's any dispute. You were appointed as police chief on the 9th of July, 1991. Is that date right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And you've told us already that you ceased to be police chief in late April 1992. In that period of time between your appointment as police chief up to the period of time you left the following year, did you report to that secretariat or Registry that you've just been talking about from time to time and told them about police matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, no. All these people from the secretariat were people from the Executive Board, and later on they were all in the Crisis Staff. So they were already privy to everything that was going on. There was no need for me to report anything about the police work because it was the majority of them in this Registry or secretariat who were decision-makers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just -- could you just explain to the Trial Chamber but more clearly, please, if you would, why you say there was no need for you to report anything about police work because the majority of them were already in the Registry or secretariat. I don't quite understand that answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When the Crisis Staff was set up after I left, there -- but there was already a Crisis Staff. After that point, for a certain period of time there was no secretariat, there was no executive committee; they were dead. The Crisis Staff and the Assembly, made up of the Serbian deputies who remained in the Assembly, the political party executive committee or Registry didn't exist at all. Only later did they resume their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm talking about not the period of time after the creation of the Crisis Staff, but the period of time between your appointment in July 1991 up until the time you left. Now, in that time did you as police chief occasionally report or hold discussions with this smaller secretariat formed from the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed chief, I immediately made it known to them that I wished my position in the SDS to be put on hold because I think that politics and my duty were incompatible. So I kind of wanted my membership to be frozen, so to say, and I refused to attend any meetings, either the executive committee or the secretariat. Well, later on it turned out that there were some lies launched against me. I appeared before the board, and I refuted all these accusations, and every time the Executive Board decided that I still have their trust and I should remain in my position, however, that I should be more diligent in providing report about my work in order to avoid all these malicious rumours going around. So on several occasions when all these rumours were widespread, I always went before them to tell them that it wasn't true. But I said that I wanted to do my job properly because it was not only the SDS who appointed me to this duty, and because it was the SDA and the HDZ endorsed my appointment. Therefore, I felt that I should be working for the well-being of everything, not only of my party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Leaving aside those explanations, did this secretariat or -- small secretariat or Registry in -- formed from the Executive Board ever seek information from you concerning police activity or police work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
