utterances.text: I don't remember attending the secretariat meetings. I may have gone to the executive committee meetings three times, let's say. And I never went to the Main Board meetings at all, but I have to say that everything important took place on the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's turn to the middle of 1991. You said -- you've told us that you were appointed in July 1991. Was there a commander of police also appointed around the same time, a gentleman named Enver Burnic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: About a month before I was appointed, he was appointed, because there were some problems. However, he was first nominated -- actually, appointed and then later on I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for that. And was he of Muslim -- was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Think now about the work that you were doing in the ensuing months after July 1991. You've told us that you met -- already this morning that you met Mr. Zupljanin some days after your appointment as police chief. At that time, what position did Mr. Zupljanin hold?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: He was my superior, and he was the head of the security services centre Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Known as the CSB -- was that the CSB regional headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when it was operated as CSB like the -- which meant security services centre because the state and the public security were together. Later on, I don't know exactly when they were separated, so it became the centre of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Leaving aside the acronyms and the bureaucracy involved, was he regional police chief in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How often did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: We had monthly meetings, regular meetings of all chiefs at his invitation, and we had to submit reports for the previous month about our work. And then quarterly, we would submit quarterly work reports, and then -- sixth-monthly report, and then annual report. As I said, we met every month. We met -- I say all the chiefs met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. In addition to the transmission of these reports, who set the agenda for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: He would send out dispatches with the agenda so that we had to prepare ourselves for the meeting. It was him who decided the topics, and we just had to prepare ourselves for the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And thinking back to those meetings, was Mr. Zupljanin a thorough man? Did he ensure that all the matters in the agenda were covered at those meetings or do his best to ensure that all matters were covered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I never noticed if something was done that wasn't on the agenda. We followed the agenda to the letter. That's how things always were. Nothing new was added; nothing was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, this system of reporting by the various police chiefs to the regional headquarters in Banja Luka, did that continue right up until late April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Individual police stations such as the Sanski Most police station, did they create daily reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to submit our reports every morning at 5.00 about all that had happened over the past 24 hours, and we sent that report to the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the report -- this daily report that you said was prepared every hour -- sorry, every day, sorry, was a copy sent to the commander of police, such as Burnic, to yourself as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same report was -- what was waiting for me in the morning on my desk and one was on the commander's desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And this sort of report, daily report, that you've just described, was -- were all the other SJB stations covered by the Banja Luka regional police area also providing such reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: That was their obligation. They had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So the CSB in Banja Luka between July and April of 1992 was receiving police information consisting of at least daily reports, information that you provided when you actually met face-to-face, quarterly reports, biannual reports, and yearly reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Up until April of -- late April of 1992, did the police in Sanski Most use teleprinters, telephones, and couriers to transmit information to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Most was done by teleprinter, by sending dispatches, because every dispatch had a marking, the marking of confidentiality, and the speed of delivery. That was one way. The second way was by couriers. The mail that had to be sent that way was sent that way. And the third way was by telephone, and that was what I used for my communication with the chief when I needed to set up meetings, when we needed to set up meetings in his office, when I asked him to receive me, because I had information for him that I had something to discuss with him or when I needed to reach some conclusions with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And those modes of communication that you've just described, were you -- you were using those modes of communication right up until the time that you left on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Turn your attention now to April of 1992. In early April of 1992, did your police station in Sanski Most receive any dispatch from a gentleman named Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I know that on the 2nd of April a dispatch came from Mr. Mandic. He was the assistant minister of the interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Assistant or deputy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Assistant. In the joint BH ministry, he was the assistant minister for crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And I want to ask you about this dispatch that you've spoken about. You've told us it came on the 2nd of April, and it was from Mandic. Was it directed just to your police station, or was it Bosnia-wide?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: It was sent to all the centres and public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Can you remember the content; and if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber basically what the content of that document was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the details. In any case, it was about the take-over of public security stations, where that was possible. That was the gist of it. Wherever possible, public security stations should have been taken over before the 15th of April. That was the gist of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber who was going to take over the public security stations. What was contemplated in the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is this: As far as I can remember, it was to the effect that wherever possible, wherever possible, public security stations should have been taken over. From Mr. Zupljanin I received several orders even before that that Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi should be left out even for a year if need be, that we should remain living together irrespective of the situation in Bosnia, that those four enclaves should be -- should continue working normally together, and that's why that dispatch did not mean that much to me. In factual terms it meant nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that explanation. But I just want to be clear about something. Public -- you said wherever possible the dispatch said, wherever possible public security stations should have been taken over. Now, leaving aside what was intended for Sanski Most, what did that -- what did you understand that to mean, that public security stations should have been taken over? Who was going to take over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: This is what was actually done. That was done where national composition was pronouncedly different, where one people was a minority with respect to the other people which was a majority. This was done spontaneously. Nobody tried to put up any resistance or whatever. I don't know. As far as I know, this was done spontaneously in the public stations in question and the hand-over was very smooth. Nobody even noticed that something had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Forgetting how smooth the hand-over was and demographic issues, all I want to know is this: Who was going to take over the public security stations according to the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Nobody had to occupy them. Within the station they had to carry out a transformation from one status to another. There was no visible take-over, just a transformation wherever that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for that. I think we're getting closer to the information I'm seeking. The transformation from one status to another mentioned in the -- or referred to or understood in the document, what change in status are we talking about here, from what to what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the Assembly of the Serbian people in the parliament - and I can't say much about that - since they took a decision sometime in March, adopted a constitution and a decision on the Ministry of the Interior, those decisions were sent to the centres and the public stations. And we were well informed about the details that were passed down from the very top. And since that was issued in the municipalities that were -- that had municipalities formed as Serbian Assemblies, there was no problem with the transfer of police from one status to another. And where the Municipal Assemblies were not in a position to make such decisions, of course that the police did not have an easy task. Things were not as simple. It was very difficult, actually, on both sides it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the dispatch refer to the creation of Serbian police stations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of that what was it called Bosnia and Herzegovina of the Serbian people, that was already an area in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the Serbian people where the Assembly of Serb MPs took a decision on the creation of such an area. That's when they adopted a constitution, the laws, the law on the interior. And that's when Mr. Mico Stanisic was appointed the minister of the then -- and we were informed about that. In dispatches he was appointed the minister of such a MUP within the area of the Serb people as they were called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you speak about this document or dispatch to anyone else in the police station when you received it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I did not want to show such dispatches to anybody. Only on the 2nd of April when we received that dispatch from Mr. Mandic, in the afternoon I went to Mr. Rasula, he was the president of the municipality, and I informed him about the dispatch that had arrived. He was taken by surprise. He didn't understand what was going on. But I didn't even want to inform anybody within the police about any such dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Although everybody in the police knew. It was on the grape-vine immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Mr. Burnic, did you speak to him about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: When I received a dispatch, a few minutes later he came to my office and asked me if I had received a dispatch. I told him, "There's no dispatch. Just proceed the way we've done so far. We will continue working within the framework of our legal obligations."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What do you mean? You told him that there -- that no dispatch existed or something else? I'm not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I told him, "There's no dispatch, no dispatch. It's not valid for me. We continue as we have done so far." On several occasions before that, Mr. Zupljanin ordered me not to do anything, that we should maintain peace, and that we should try and curb all the national tensions in the municipality, that we should not allow them to get off the ground. And then Mr. Burnic, even before Zupljanin told me that, Burnic told me that it had been decided that the four municipalities would remain enclaves and that nothing would be going on here in terms of the take-over, we would remain oasis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on I heard that from Mr. Zupljanin who warned me about that and he told me how to behave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Take it slower if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 62, please. Is it possible to get the English up?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's just have a look first at this document. I think you've seen this before. This is not the dispatch that you've just been speaking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's dated the 31st of March, 1992, and you can see it goes to all public security stations and the SDB, the State Security Service, and all security services centres. In -- the first paragraph, as you can see, describes various political and legal developments, and I'm interested in asking you questions about the third -- well, what appears in the B/C/S as the second paragraph headed -- and above that page 2, little number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if we could scroll down on the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just have a read of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if we could also scroll down to the bottom with the English. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2, do you want me to read the paragraph on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, just read it to yourself. I'll ask you questions about that. The document is signed by Deputy Minister of the Interior, Momcilo Mandic. And it says that public security stations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are abolished and their tasks and duties are taken over by the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you see that? And finally in the paragraph it says that prior to engagement of -- these new bodies, employees are obliged to swear an oath of allegiance before the minister or an official. Is there anything in that document sent to the SJBs that is inconsistent with the dispatch that you received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know. I don't understand you. Are you referring to this as compared to Mr. Mandic's dispatch dated the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm comparing this document here signed by Momcilo Mandic, and asking you to compare it with the dispatch that you've spoken about. This document is -- can you tell the Trial Chamber if this document is consistent with the information that you read and saw in the dispatch that you have told us about this morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The dispatch dated the 2nd of April that arrived and that was signed by Mr. Momcilo Mandic was shorter than this one, of course. It may have been half a page. I found it very strange. What I'm reading now and what I remember from before, I know that that dispatch looked very strange to me, and that's why perhaps I just put it in my pocket. And when my commander came, I just told him, "Just proceed the way we're doing now." And it differed from this dispatch here, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sure the documents are different. You've already told us they are different. You told us that, we know that. Thank you. What I'm asking you is this: Is this document basically consistent with the dispatch that you received? In other words, this document refers to the abolishment of public security stations for the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the -- where they appear on territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I've told you already several times that I don't remember exactly, but it differed in the style. It looked like an order, an order to do something that differs a lot from what I am reading now. The essence of the two was different. Globally speaking, there was some similar characteristics, but the style was different, and it was -- I found it very strange. And I really can't find any grounds of comparison between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please, I seek to tender the document. If there's going to be an objection I will ask that it be marked for identification and another witness can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. The witness did not identify this as something that he received. He did not recognise the content. There is not enough nexus to introduce this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I join my colleague Krgovic. I believe it's impossible to use this witness as an appropriate witness to clarify the ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Mandic is also on the list of Prosecutor's witnesses, so maybe my learned friend, Mr. Di Fazio, can face Mr. Mandic with this document and try and seek clarification with him as regards to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, inasmuch as Mr. Di Fazio is content to have it marked for identification, we do that at this stage. And, Mr. Di Fazio, this is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's a good time for me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P353, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, may I raise or alert you to a possible scheduling issue because I think I have to take some of the blame, it took a little longer with the last witness than I thought it would take. I understand now based on the estimated time for Defence cross-examination that with a normal sitting day on Monday we may not finish with this witness, and I think on Tuesday the videolink witness has to take priority. We've discussed with the Defence they don't object to interrupting his testimony and proceeding with the videolink as scheduled. The witness I think has been alerted to this possibility. He doesn't mind staying here and finishing his testimony on Thursday or Friday if need be. If that pleases Your Honours, that's what we would propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm sorry, but I'm -- I get very frustrated when -- your -- the document we just marked was 65 ter 62; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, I get very frustrated when I can't find it on your list of documents to use -- for use with this witness. Can you assist me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I can't. My case manager alerted me earlier to the fact that it wasn't on the list, and it should have been on the list. It was always in my contemplation to use it and it's my responsibility entirely, and I have to accept responsibility for that. I hadn't realised it wasn't on the list. I had assumed that it being one of the first documents I was going to use that it was on the list. So I have to apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll try and ensure that that doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or if it happens, Mr. Di Fazio, it would be of assistance if you can say that it isn't on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is on the list. Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 76, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Majkic, this is a document that was sent to all SJB stations or on the face of it was apparently sent to all SJB stations and appears to be a document of Mr. Zupljanin, although it's unsigned. In the -- could you just have a quick look at the -- sorry, and it's dated the 10th of April, 1992, so not long after the dispatch that you've spoken about earlier. And the document refers to a dispatch communication that -- an earlier dispatch communication about forced formation of organisational units of the Serb MUP. And then it goes on to say that there's no -- I'll withdraw that. Yes, then it goes on to say that there are -- that there is -- in the formation of organisational units, there is no forcing. And then it goes on in the second paragraph to talk about employees needing to sign a formal statement, and this should be no different from the statement of the ex-minister of internal affairs and should have nothing to do with the so-called statement of loyalty noted in the dispatch. Firstly, have you seen this document before? Do you recall receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The title or the address is to the SJB chief and commander to all SJB chiefs and commanders, that means that I must have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the format. Look at the format, not what the content of the document is but the format, what it looks like visually. Is that the sort of format of -- or one of the formats of documents sent to various SJB stations by Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The A4 format is a normal format. All such letters and dispatches were sent on the A4 format papers, and I believe that this is A4 format, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall actually receiving any such document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it says that it was sent to all the SJB chiefs and commanders, which means that I must have received it. But I can't recall this. There were a host of such dispatches. I can't recall this particular one, but I must have received it judging by the address.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic, you were about to raise an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Identical as before. The witness cannot recall the document, cannot recognise the document, cannot interpret its contents. Maybe this document should be introduced through another witness. Again, the same objection as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I understood the witness's testimony to be is that unlike the previous document that he must have received this one. So wouldn't that have -- wouldn't that put it in a different category?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's your decision. I just raised my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, the document is not signed. Is it a Telex, or what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's a Telex, if Your Honours please, or if it was a typed document. Perhaps we could ask the witness himself. He might be -- he's probably in the best position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You heard His Honour's question. Looking at the document, what does it tell you, that this was a Telex or sent by fax or letter, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I've just spotted in the address to the SJB, to all chiefs and commanders, I am not sure. It doesn't really make sense for the chief of the security services centre to send this dispatch both to the chiefs and to the commanders. Normally such dispatches would only be sent to the chiefs. And as for the manner of sending, I don't know. I don't know whether it was sent by teleprinter, whether it was typed and sent by some other media. I really -- I can't say anything for sure. I wouldn't be able to tell you what method of sending was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just ask -- I apologise. Can I ask just one more question of the witness that might assist in this topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you recall there being any controversy or issue concerning whether or not the creation of the Serbian MUP was to be forced or whether it was to be voluntary? Can you remember that being an issue and being raised in paperwork in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You will have to repeat because I did not arrive at understanding the question the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Look, the document says -- refers to a previous dispatch. You told us about that earlier today. And it talks about having -- police having been informed about forced formation of organisational units. And the author, apparent author Mr. Zupljanin, goes on to warn that the formation of organisational units is not forced in any way. Now, can you recall - regardless of what this document says - but can you recall if in April of 1992 there was any concern or controversy in police circles about that issue, that very issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I've already told you several times and I have repeated several times, the status of Sanski Most, Kljuc, Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi were explained to me by Mr. Zupljanin on several occasions. He spoke about our status in the future as well. So I was not much bothered. I was not interested in the dispatches or information with such context. I really did not give such things any second thought. Even if I received such kind of instructions or dispatches, I would just ignore them because they actually did not apply to me. And why would Mr. Zupljanin tell me one thing and then send me an entirely different thing? It doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We recall the order marking it as an exhibit and will now have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is pending authentication through another witness who is able to speak more directly to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the purposes of the transcript, this is Exhibit P354 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In 1992, did you become aware of an organisation in Sanski Most bearing the acronym SOS and standing for Serbian Defence Force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, the existence of the SOS, Serbian Defence Forces, was the first time mentioned at the meeting of the 14th of April, that is the meeting of the executive committee where they appeared with a sort of ultimatum. I think that this was more of a fantasy made by people in town. They used to tell stories about this small group of young men. We assumed there were seven or eight of them. And we used to call them SOS men. Prior to that, we had no information about any organisation and existence. To put it simply, people were talking in the town about the SOS. As for the police, the police had no information about their being formed. Only on the 14th of April when they appeared for the first time before the executive committee with the ultimatum of taking over the public security station was when I saw these three men for the first time, and they declared themselves or introduced themselves as members of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your position that the police in Sanski Most had no information or intelligence about SOS or SOS activities in Sanski Most up until the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: There was mention of that organisation in the police as well, just like among ordinary people, in the same way. We had some suspicions that there were these seven or eight lads. Later on, when I saw that there were about 50 of them, then I realised that they were a rather serious and larger organisation because we had no idea that they had such strengths. We thought that they were self-styled organisation, member numbering seven or eight people. So we acted according to the stories that reached us from the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So the police were gathering intelligence, I assume, or information about them and concluded that there were about seven or eight of them, local Sanski Most lads?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: That's what we in the police concluded, that there were no more than seven and eight of them. We suspected of certain crimes being committed by them, and then we engaged all our resources in order to try and catch them in flagrante in committing these crimes, but we never managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what sort of crimes were these?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Usually planting of explosives in certain Muslim and Croat buildings, but in three occasions they attacked the buildings owned by the Serbs. However, they caused only damage but there were no casualties. And the damage was insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And were these bombings occurring in late 1991 and also early 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Precisely in that period, autumn of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, so four or five months all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that these crimes were investigated. Did the police ever get any results, and by that I mean solve the crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The police and the investigating judge and the prosecutor would always visit the crime scene, do what they were supposed to do, criminal reports were being filed, but we never managed to detect who the perpetrators were, although I also ordered the commander as well to take part with the police in on-site investigation and to become involved in the detection process of these crimes. Therefore, we had quite a few people involved in these investigations, but as I say, we never succeeded in solving these crimes or proving who the perpetrators were. Although the suspicion was always there, that this was exactly those young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So your police had suspicions that the SOS was involved in these bombings throughout 1991 and 1992. The police must therefore have paid particular attention to the SOS and done its utmost to investigate the SOS, this group of seven or eight lads from Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were the police able to get information about these seven or eight lads in Sanski Most, for example, where they lived, who they were, what they were doing in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The two who we thought were the ring-leaders used to be sportsmen, they played hand-ball, however, they didn't have any criminal records or even misdemeanour records in the police. So we were a little perplexed about that, that all of a sudden such a law-abiding citizen started committing crimes. Therefore, we carried out this thorough investigation in order to detect them and prove anything, but as I said, we failed. Either they were too skilful or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll come back to the Sanski Most SOS in a while. In early April 1992, did you go to Banja Luka and attend a meeting with -- where Mr. Zupljanin was present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it took place on the 6th of April. He sent a dispatch inviting us to come to this meeting three or four days before that, and he included an agenda for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this -- on this occasion did Mr. Zupljanin explain to you that the SOS had taken over Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The meeting took place on the 6th of April, but on the morning of the 4th of April on Radio Banja Luka on some other local radio I heard that the Serbian Defence Forces in Banja Luka had carried out a sort of assault or whatever and took power. Then Mr. Zupljanin informed us about this piece of news at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the 6th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That was the first you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I said I first heard it on the radio on the 4th of April, on the day it happened. It happened on the early morning of the 4th of April when the SOS carried out this act, and when I came to the meeting on the 6th of April Mr. Zupljanin told us the same story about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the radio provide information to citizens in the area that it was the SOS that had taken over Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They even said that they were called the Serbian Defence Forces and that they were the ones who took over power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Well, now given the fact that police in Sanski Most had suspected the SOS of carrying out bombing attacks in Sanski Most, and considering that you knew because you'd heard it on the radio that they'd supposedly taken over Banja Luka, was this issue of the activities of the SOS discussed -- sorry, on the agenda of the meeting that you went to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Zupljanin informed us about this act of theirs and what had happened. That was at the very beginning of the meeting. He told us what had happened in Banja Luka. And he commented nothing further about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's all he said, just that they -- the SOS have taken over Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that they had carried out this act of take-over of power, and that in fact the power in Banja Luka had changed hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This must have been a source of serious concern to you, given the fact that you - as chief of police in Sanski Most and the police in Sanski Most - suspected the SOS of carrying out bombing attacks throughout the latter part of 1991 and into 1992 and now they were taking over Banja Luka. So that must have been a source of absolute concern to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but these SOS forces, as far as I know -- or actually, I'm convinced 100 per cent, they were not at the government level. They were rather some local organisations. There were some towns that, for example, needed these kind of forces. This is where they were formed. For example, the SOS in Sanski Most and the one in Banja Luka had no connection. They didn't cooperate with each other. They had their own respective plans and operated according to those plans. They had their own agendas that they pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Explain to the Trial Chamber, please, where you obtained information about the agenda and plans of the SOS in Sanski Most. Where did you get that from? How did you know it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, it was a Monday, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about the 6th of April. The 6th of April at the meeting. Where did you have the information about the SOS and its leadership and its plans -- from where had you obtained that information as at the 6th of April when you were sitting in the room there with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I already said Mr. Zupljanin informed us about this act. That's all. It was a very brief information, and nobody discussed this any longer. The meeting went on according to its established agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which did not include anything about the SOS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what the agenda was, but if this take-over of power in Banja Luka took place on the 4th and we arrived on the 6th and we received the invitation before the 4th containing the agenda, it is most probable that some items on the agenda had been added to the agenda following the events of Banja Luka, maybe to involve those berets and tri-colours and the uniforms that were mentioned were probably included into the agenda by Mr. Zupljanin as something that had a bearing on the events in Banja Luka. So probably that was the outcome of what happened on the 4th April. Of course the agenda that we had originally received with the dispatch, we worked on it. I can only understand that probably the agenda was amended by adding some additional topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that Mr. Zupljanin merely announced that the SOS had taken over Banja Luka, and given the fact that you and police in Sanski Most had suspicions that an organisation also named SOS had been responsible for bombings in Sanski Most, did it not occur to you to raise the issue with your regional chief and indeed with all the other police chiefs and explain that a very serious problem was developing with SOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honours. I didn't intervene before. I don't -- in principle don't have any problems with the line of questioning that my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio is posing, but the formulation of the questions and -- sometimes they're multi-folded, they are loaded, and they are leading questions at the end. So I kindly ask to either split questions or be underlining like he usually excellent is doing in examination-in-chief. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. I'll reduce it to one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the leading questions, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you raise the question of the bombings at this meeting on the 6th of April with your regional chief, bombings in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: At each meeting when I submitted my monthly reports, I always highlighted these crimes or any other crimes that had happened, just like we did on a daily basis if need be. But we only had suspicion about these young men, these SOS or however they called themselves. We had our suspicions. We didn't want to pressure them and to flush them out; we wanted to call them at -- catch them red-handed. But I did report any crime at our regular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You had driven from Sanski Most to this meeting on the 6th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you were in a police car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, always in a police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And you're able to enter Banja Luka and go to the meeting no problem I assume?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: At this point I cannot recall, but when I was travelling on the 6th I don't think that I saw any check-points along the way on my way to Banja Luka or perhaps I've forgotten. I really don't remember. All I know is that I didn't encounter any problems on my way to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So it was a -- as far as you were concerned, a smooth ride into Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you make inquiries of the original police chief, Mr. Zupljanin, or any of the other police chiefs as to what SOS taking over actually involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was already a fait accompli. Under the pressure of the SOS, the power changed hands. For me coming from Sanski Most was something that was a fait accompli. Probably Mr. Zupljanin behaved afterwards in keeping with what the government or the local governments of these taken-over municipalities had agreed with him. But I know nothing about that; therefore, I'm not the right person to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks, and thanks for that explanation about power changes and so on. But my question is very simple. You apparently had a smooth ride into Banja Luka and yet you are informed, A, by the radio; and B, by your regional police chief that the SOS had taken over. In those circumstances, did you consider getting information about what precisely was involved in the take-over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Since this took place on Saturday, it was a non-working day, on the Monday I went to Banja Luka - and since this was an ongoing process not only in Banja Luka but in other municipalities as well - it sort of became something normal. I'm not saying normal, but kind of -- it became a frequent occurrence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this way of taking over power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You said that Mr. Zupljanin said nothing more about the take-over of power other than to announce the fact of it. Did you or any other policemen offer any solutions as to what you might do to ensure that the SOS were disarmed, arrested, placed into prison, and order restored? Was that discussed by you or any other policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you. This SOS, we assumed that this was a kind of paramilitary armed force of a considerable size and we were not sure whether the police was fit to enter into any conflict with them. Perhaps it was only the military capable of doing that, and I very much doubt that the police was capable of doing anything to counter the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what it is -- sorry. Explain to the Trial Chamber how you and the police and why you and the police assumed that the SOS was a paramilitary armed force of considerable size. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that in Sanski Most when the war started and when they were disbanded, we never found out who set up this organisation and how. We never learned where they had come from --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: -- the same applied to Banja Luka. There was no one standing behind the SOS organisation, not even the SDS. Quite simply, it was a paramilitary organisation and how they organised themselves was never clear to me to this date --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine, fine --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: -- all I know is that there was no one behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Well, that's some intelligence about the SOS that you had. Given that intelligence, can you explain to the Trial Chamber where the assumption comes - assumption - that this SOS was a paramilitary force of considerable size? Where did that -- on what was that assumption based, the assumption you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: We didn't know that until they appeared in reality or in practice with this act of taking over power in Banja Luka or when they came at the meeting in Sanski Most with this ultimatum that power should be transferred to them. We had no other information. We didn't know who was behind them. We -- all we knew was that they were a paramilitary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Majkic, I haven't finished yet with the 6th of April meeting, but just leave it for a moment. Given what you had been told by Mr. Zupljanin in -- on the -- at the 6th of April meeting and given your suspicions of the SOS in Sanski Most being involved in bomb-throwing campaigns or throwing of bombs, did you go back to Sanski Most and continue to investigate the activities of the SOS in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: If a criminal report had been filed against an unidentified perpetrator, that means that there is an ongoing search for these perpetrators. It was already April, but I think that this stopped sometime in mid-March, but nevertheless the police had an obligation to investigate such crimes until they uncover the perpetrators, for as long as it takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking you is that given what you discovered in Banja Luka and were informed in Banja Luka, did you -- did that provide any incentive to go back and investigate more thoroughly, more deeply, the activities of the SOS in Sanski Most; and if so, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 6th, when the meeting ended sometime in the afternoon I arrived home in the evening. I didn't go back to the office because the office hours were over. And on that day, between the 6th and the 7th, the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived in Sanski Most. And the troops were deployed on the hilltops and all over the place. I don't know what their employment schedule was, but in any case the brigade was deployed there on the 7th of April. That's when I met Colonel Basara. We had coffee together. He came to me and told me, "I arrived to prevent international inter-ethnic conflicts." Given the fact that in mid-March those inter-ethnic tensions started mounting -- in Sanski Most I experienced some personal problems because I was involved in curbing those inter-ethnic tensions and I was successful to some extent. However, in mid-March I sent a letter to the 5th Corps and the commander of the 6th Brigade, Basara, asking for the 6th Sana Brigade to return to Sanski Most after having spent a lot of time on the front line because I expected there would be imminent inter-ethnic conflicts in Sanski Most. According to the information that I had from people in the army who had told me later about that, Colonel Basara took this letter on several occasions to the corps commander asking him to allow him to attend to Sanski Most. This was approved some 20 days later, and he returned to Sanski Most together with the brigade. And that was done because the inter-ethnic tensions had been mounting in Sanski Most for some time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I didn't actually ask you about that, but you raised that issue of the 6th Brigade returning. Did they provide any reassurance to you in dealing with groups like the SOS in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Again, I repeat. In Sanski Most the SOS did not exist. Nobody knew about it. Those were all suspicions by -- on the part of the citizens, on the part of the police. There were, as we assumed, only six or seven lads. We didn't have a clue that the group was actually much bigger than only perhaps six or seven of them. I really don't know. I'm a bit -- I don't know. I don't know what I actually wanted to say. I'm a bit confused now. The existence of the SDS was nowhere on paper. It was never made official. It was never in writing. Nothing. We tried to detect the perpetrators of crime, but we failed. We never made any progress. We can't be sure to this very day that they were the ones who did all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll return to Mr. Basara and the SOS later. Just let's go back now to the 6th of April meeting. On -- you've told us that Mr. Zupljanin mentioned the take-over and that was it. What else did he discuss with you police chiefs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: It was probably reports. It was the beginning of the month. We had to submit our reports, and after that he spoke about the berets, the markings on the berets, the solemn declarations. One uniform was hanging on the coat rack in the corner. He showed us that uniform as a model of what the uniforms would like under new circumstances. That was discussed, and at the end he distributed the berets, the markings for the berets, and the solemn declarations. I received some hundred of the berets and some hundred of the solemn declarations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just tell us about these berets. What exactly were they, what were they intended for, and what insignia did they contain or have on them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: The berets were blue, very standard issue. It could have been any colour, but it was blue. And the insignia on the berets were a metal three-coloured Serbian flags, and they're supposed to be put on the berets, the flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what did he say should be done with these berets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: When the transformation had already been completed of the police forces in the municipalities and when new conditions were in place with keeping with the constitution and the laws that had been adopted by the Assembly of the Serbian People, those berets were given to those municipalities. They did give them to me also, but then Mr. Zupljanin told me Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, as I've already told you five times and he said to me at least five times, you shouldn't do anything in these municipalities be it as long as it may -- even a year. So what I did with the berets is I put them in the trunk of my car, never showed them to anybody, only when the conditions changed in Sanski Most I took them out and distributed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks for explaining that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could you think of winding up between 1.30 and 1.35. There's a procedural matter which Mr. Zecevic wishes to raise before we adjourn, and then the Chamber itself has a short matter with which to deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours, perhaps if I just deal with this particular meeting, that would probably be a natural break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, if you think of 1.35 as the outside time for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So -- sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me. I just want to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Zupljanin told you that in various municipalities, including yours, some -- you shouldn't do anything in these municipalities. Did you know what was going to happen in the other municipalities, that he was -- the ones he wasn't referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I did not even think about what would be happening in the other municipalities. I was only concerned with the security of my and sanctity of my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And he said that you shouldn't do anything in particular with the berets, and only when conditions changed you took them out and distributed them. Was that by pre-arrangement? Did you know what sort of conditions had to apply before you could use the berets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin distributed those to all the chiefs where the transformation had been carried out. I received them too. I don't know whether the berets were also given to the Prijedor chief. I can't be sure of that. But I know that everybody was given or should have been given all the berets. Zupljanin distributed them to everybody, including myself, but then again he repeated, "You do not take any steps even for as long as a year. Stay put. Don't do anything." And he mentioned Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi as the municipalities that should not be affected by the distribution of the berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. The steps that you just spoke about, don't take any steps even for as long as a year he said, stay put. Now, did you understand what steps Mr. Zupljanin was referring to you when he said to you, "Don't take any steps, even for as long as a year"? What were those steps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: If the chief told me not to do anything, he told that to me, he ordered me not to do anything, no steps, nothing, nothing. He just said, "Continue doing what you have done so far. You will be an oasis in Bosnia-Herzegovina where people will live in peace, in unity, as you have in the past." That's the way I understood him and that's the way I behaved, according to his instructions or orders. You call them what you will. I don't know what to call his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. But in order for you to have had a sensible discussion, you must have understood what the steps were that he was talking about when he said to you, "Mr. Majkic, don't take any steps in Sanski Most." So explain to the Trial Chamber what were the steps that you two had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Nobody had any intention to do something. Nobody had any intention to take over. Even if I took the 2nd of April dispatch to Mr. Rasula, he was taken by surprise. He was the top man in the municipality, and he agreed with what Mr. Zupljanin said. Because we found that a most convenient thing in Sanski Most and we behaved normally, we worked normally, together until the very last day, until the moment there was an agreement on division. And when we parted our own ways, until that very day we worked together as if everything was normal. The police force was united as if nothing was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Did he also have oaths, loyalty oaths, printed out on paper and did he distribute those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he have a uniform which he showed to you police chiefs as an example of a new uniform that was to be worn by police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: There was just one uniform hanging on the clothes rack in the corner -- but not really in the corner. It was actually next to the desk at which he was sitting together with the other leaders from the centre. He stood up and he showed us the uniform, he pointed to it and said that that was the kind of uniform that policemen should wear. There was just one sample, that one uniform hanging on the coat rack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can you just describe it, please, to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: There was a beret, and since it was April or already warm there was a blue camouflage shirt and there was also a pair of trousers with pockets on the side. It was also a blue pattern similar to the military camouflage uniform. The police uniform would have been similar, not the same but very similar. It was a camouflage uniform but the colour was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Let's just wrap this topic up quickly, if you could keep your answers as short as possible. Did you eventually -- sorry, did you take possession of your berets, your copies of loyalty oaths, put them in your car, and eventually drive back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. I didn't hear that the witness mentioned a word "loyalty oaths."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This witness simply said "oaths."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you put the oaths on paper and the berets and -- into your car and drive back to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you distribute the berets and the oaths on paper when you got back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I hid them well. I didn't want somebody to steal them. I had thought that I would not be needing them in a while, in a long while.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you hide them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: In the trunk of my car, and the car was only driven by me and that's where I hid them, in the trunk. And my car was always in the garage that was locked, and only when I used it I would take it out of the garage and then I would drive it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And just the actual content of the oath, in fact, what was the oath on that -- printed out on that paper that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC
utterances.text: It was a solemn declaration. The title was "solemn declaration." I know that the contents were the same as the contents of the former solemn declaration that we used to take before 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was identical. The only difference being a reference to Republika Srpska and the Serbian people. I can't really give you the exact details of those changes. Everything else, the rest of the contents, were absolutely the same as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time on this topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We must take the adjournment for today, and we will resume with your testimony on Monday, Monday morning. You having been sworn as a witness, you cannot communicate with the lawyers from either side; and in such conversations that you have with anybody outside of the chamber, you can't discuss your testimony before the Tribunal. Do you understand what I've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, thank you, sir. You're now excused, and we wish you a safe weekend, and we will see you on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before I hear you, we have a ruling to deliver, and that is that -- this is an oral decision on the Prosecution's notices on the mode of testimony of SD-4, 52, and 140. On the 28th of October, the Trial Chamber granted the Defence until the 11th of November to respond regarding requests of the Prosecution filed as notices on the 14th and 26th of October to amend the mode of testimony of witnesses 4, 52, and 140. The Prosecution requests that these witnesses testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In addition, the Prosecution seeks to add to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list 20 documents relating to the witnesses. Also on the 28th of October, the Chamber granted a similar request regarding ST-79 and allow the Prosecution to add to its exhibit list three documents relating to this witness. The Defence did not file any request by the 11th of November. The Prosecution submits there is no prejudice to the accused as a result of the variation of the mode of testimony of ST-4, 52, and 140. It argues that the transcripts, written statements, and associated exhibits meet the requirements of admissibility under the rules and that the amendments of the mode of testimony are made in an attempt to save court time and to stream-line the presentation of evidence. The Prosecution submits that the 20 documents form an inseparable part of the witness's prior evidence. The Prosecution submits that ST-4 will be testifying about police involvement in crimes. 52 is a crime base witness and 140 is a linkage witness. Considering the nature of the testimony of the witnesses, the Trial Chamber finds that the witnesses should be present in court to attest the accuracy of their prior statements and be available for cross-examining judicial questioning pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the evidence of the witnesses fulfil the requirements of Rule 92 ter. It is recalled that the parties' witnesses and exhibit lists can only be amended with leave of the Trial Chamber upon showing of good cause of the requesting party. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the 20 documents form an inextricable and indispensable part of witnesses' evidence. It also notes that there is no objection from the Defence. The Chamber therefore allows the Prosecution to call ST-4, ST-52, and ST-140 pursuant to Rule 92 ter. It will accept on to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit lists ST-4's prior statement, ST-52's prior statements and 11 associated documents, and ST-140's prior statements and testimonies and nine associates documents. This material will be admitted into evidence upon the witnesses having complied with the conditions of Rule 92 ter. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I wish to raise a matter which is of great concern for the Defence, and actually the last question and the answer of the witness gave me a perfect pretext. Now, Your Honours, when my friend Mr. Di Fazio showed the document P353, which was MFI'd, he mentioned in the document when he was -- he was directing the witness, he mentioned the oath of allegiance, and I -- and I was wondering where did that come from. Now I checked the document. The document, Serbian original, says clearly "solemn declaration," like it was interpreted here in court Svecana Obaveza means solemn declaration, so there was no oath whatsoever mentioned in the document. Now, the translation of that document is clearly wrong, and I was always wondering where did the idea -- the allegation, which is an issue in this case, of a loyalty oath, of oath of allegiance, of any kind of oath came to the -- came as an idea for the Office of the Prosecutor because I never ever in all the documents which were disclosed in this case ever found anything suggesting oath or anything of a kind. It was always a solemn declaration, which does not mean an oath like over here. The witnesses are giving the solemn declaration. They are not taking an oath. Now, my submission is that I would ask the Trial Chamber to order that this document, 353, be sent to the CLSS for official review of the translation so that in future we don't have any more of this -- because this is not the proper allegation. It is only the misinterpretation which led the Office of the Prosecutor to allege that there was some -- any kind of oath taken and something like that. And I think -- I think this is of help for all the parties that we do not use the time -- the court time improperly by making objections and that we clarify this situation once and for all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber wishes to thank you for drawing our attention to these problems. It's very useful that you have done so, and we urge counsels consistently to take up any difficulties that they may become aware of regarding translation. It -- it is of course of no secret that translations as well as interpretations will occasionally incur inaccuracies, although I believe generally that the services we have at our disposal, both for interpretation and also for translations, are of a very high standard. But of course we are dealing with human beings and inaccuracies or mistakes do occur, and that's why it's important that you who speak the language draw our attention to it. In the instant case, I suggest we ask translation -- the CLSS to have a look at it and then take whatever measures are required accordingly. So if we can ask Madam Registrar to bring this to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours, I understand, and I appreciate, and I just didn't mean to criticise either CLSS or interpreters. It's just a mistake which I didn't say was intentionally made. It's just that this mistake has misleaded our friends from the Prosecution for their allegations. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just very shortly, and as usual our friends from Prosecution like to be sort of misleaded and they create their own theory, and, you know, that's why we have to clarify all these issues in order to have very precise proceedings. Your Honours, just very briefly, I would like to respectfully bring to our attention our old motion when Honourable Judge Harhoff was a Pre-Trial Judge sometimes in June. Actually, 3.000 documents from -- which was seized from CSB Banja Luka police regional centre in 1998 are still not available to the Defence. I would call this issue, issue 3.000. As far as I remember, we filed a joint motion with that regard. The position of the OTP was that for certain public reasons, security reasons, or whatsoever we were not allowed to have access to these documents. So we discussed that in details, Judge Harhoff I believe is aware about that. Now we are most -- more than -- let's say -- we are almost two months in trial and you can imagine, Your Honours, that -- I don't want to speculate, but maybe some of these 3.000 documents might be of certain importance for the Defence. So I just want to bring to your attention to see where we are in this issue about the motion that we filed with respect to these documents, 3.000 documents, and what would be the position of the OTP with that regard. I mean, I'm not asking immediate resolution, but just to put on the record that I think that we have to deal with that issue. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, would you like to give a reply or comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I would need to be able to look at the -- refresh my memory and look at the motion and our response in order to be able to comment in any way that would assist you, and I can't do that as I stand here. If Your Honours please, the matter can be addressed on Monday. I can raise it with my colleagues, and I think that's probably the easiest and best way of going about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm just being instructed or being reminded by our Legal Officer that the issue is under consideration in the Chamber and that we will hand down our ruling shortly. And so I don't think -- we have heard already the submissions by the Prosecution, so there is no need to bring -- unless of course you have anything new to add. But otherwise the decision is due to arrive very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sure the matter has been well ventilated in the motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have one short matter to discuss as well. The time estimates again. I was told that we got your time estimates for the witnesses that are expected to come before Christmas from the Defence counsels. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have the estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And we have them as well. You have communicated them to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because we were waiting for some witnesses which -- we want to give you the complete list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Because we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we still haven't had the time to check all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
